articles.title: Email threat landscape: Q3 2026 trends and insights
articles.context: In September, purchase order and payroll lures used disguised archives to deliver Agent Tesla, malware commonly used to collect credentials and other information
articles.full_text:
In this article

Spoofed sender domains

QR code phishing attacks

CAPTCHA-gated phishing tactics

Malicious payloads

Business contact impersonation

Microsoft Teams threats

Notable phishing campaigns

Defending against email and collaboration threats

Hunting queries

Indicators of compromise (IOCs)

Microsoft Threat Intelligence detected approximately 7.3 billion email-based phishing threats from July through September, including a sharp increase to nearly 3 billion in September alone, up 41% from August. Yet the increase did not extend across the techniques that had driven threat actor activity earlier in the year. QR code phishing remained far below its early-year peak, while CAPTCHA-gated phishing reversed several months of decline, driven in part by renewed use of SVG attachments.

Q2 in review

Shifting tactics and other trends ›

Figure 1. Monthly detected email threat volume (January – September 2026)

The quarter also highlighted how sender identity and security exceptions can shape the outcome of detected threats. Microsoft detected approximately 129 million malicious messages spoofing the sender domains of tracked business services. Many were delivered because organization- or user-configured exceptions overrode security protections, even after the messages failed authentication checks and were identified as malicious, showing how overly broad exceptions intended to preserve legitimate workflows can also expose them to impersonation. In Microsoft Teams, attackers increasingly used ordinary personal names rather than explicit help desk identities while continuing to use live interactions for social engineering. Across malicious attachment activity more broadly, credential theft remained the dominant objective in Q3.

Two campaigns observed during the quarter illustrate the range of activity behind these trends. An August campaign targeting legal organizations used personalized salary review documents and QR codes to lead recipients into device code phishing, despite the broader decline in QR code attacks. In September, purchase order and payroll lures used disguised archives to deliver Agent Tesla, malware commonly used to collect credentials and other information. Together, the campaigns show how familiar business requests remained effective lures across distinct attack paths.

TYCOON2FA

Inside the PhaaS platform ›

The effects of the March disruption of the Tycoon2FA phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) platform also remained evident. By July, Microsoft detected approximately 21,000 phishing messages linked to the platform, down 99.8% from 8.9 million in February, the last full month before the operation.

Figure 2. Tycoon2FA-linked phishing email volume (January 2026 – July 2026)

This blog provides a view of email threat activity across Q3 2026, examining shifts in phishing techniques, malicious payloads, business contact impersonation (BCI), and Teams-based threats. We also highlight spoofed business-service sender domains and two campaigns that show how attackers used familiar work requests to make malicious messages appear credible. Together with recommendations, Microsoft Defender detections, and hunting queries, these findings can help defenders assess where existing protections may be weakened and investigate activity across email and collaboration platforms.

Spoofed sender domains

Requests to sign a document, review an invoice, or respond to a survey are routine business communications. Attackers exploit that familiarity by spoofing the sender domains of the legitimate services that deliver them. Rather than relying only on a misleading display name or a lookalike domain, these messages claim the service’s actual domain as their sender identity.

Microsoft detected approximately 129 million malicious messages spoofing the business-service domains tracked in this analysis during Q3. Activity had remained consistently high since at least May, at roughly 41 million to 46 million messages a month. DocuSign was the most frequently spoofed brand in September, accounting for 29% of that month’s total. Adobe, SurveyMonkey, and Barracuda also saw increases toward the end of the quarter, even as overall spoofing volume remained broadly steady.

Figure 3. Malicious messages spoofing tracked business-service sender domains (May – September 2026)

The more consequential finding was how security exceptions affected these messages after detection. Despite failing email authentication checks and being identified as malicious, many were associated with tenant- or user-level overrides. In September, overrides applied to 63% of messages with a recorded security outcome, with tenant-level overrides accounting for most of them.

The figures do not establish that recipients opened the messages or that accounts were compromised. They do show why exception policies deserve attention alongside detection coverage. An organization may create an exception to avoid interrupting a legitimate business workflow, but an overly broad exception can also weaken protection against messages impersonating that workflow. Familiar branding is not a substitute for an authenticated sender.

QR code phishing attacks

QR code phishing ended Q3 far below the levels seen during its early-year surge. Microsoft detected approximately 12.1 million attacks over the quarter, down 67% from Q2. The decline continued through September despite the broader increase in email threats, leaving monthly QR code volume 86% below its March peak.

Figure 4. Monthly QR code phishing volume (January – September 2026)

Much of the volume reduction came from the attachments that had supported that earlier growth:

PDF attachments remained the most common delivery format in Q3, accounting for 78% of QR code attacks in July and August before dropping to 61% in September. Nonetheless, the volume of PDFs carrying malicious QR codes fell by roughly 65% by the end of the quarter.

DOC/DOCX attachments accounted for 14% of QR code attacks in July and August before rising to 20% in September. Word document delivery volume similarly contracted in Q3, falling 39% between July and September following a sharp drop at the start of the quarter.

Email-embedded QR codes increased from 5% of attacks in July to 12% in September. After dropping to near-zero in Q2, the volume of malicious QR codes embedded in email bodies more than tripled by the end of Q3, although the method remained a smaller delivery category than attachments.

Figure 5. QR code phishing delivery method share by month (January – September 2026)

The distinction between delivery methods matters for inspection coverage, but not for the recipient’s experience: either attachment or embedded formats can move a user from a message on a managed device to a phishing page on a personal phone. The reduction in volume has not changed that underlying challenge.

CAPTCHA-gated phishing tactics

CAPTCHA-gated phishing began to recover while QR code attacks continued to fall. By September, Microsoft detected 3.1 million CAPTCHA-gated attacks, nearly twice the volume seen at July’s low. Activity remained well below its March peak, but the recovery ended several months of sustained decline.

Figure 6. CAPTCHA-gated phishing volume (January – September 2026)

The increase in CAPTCHA-gated phishing attacks was not confined to a single attachment format as delivery methods shifted throughout Q3, though SVG attachments were central to the initial recovery.

SVG attachment volume increased sixfold in August, accounting for almost half of September’s total CAPTCHA-gated phishing attacks. Up from 17% of attacks in July, SVGs represented 65% of CAPTCHA-gated phishing attacks in August, remained elevated at 49% in September, and were the leading delivery method at the quarter end.

Email-embedded URLs accounted for 49% of attacks in July before falling to 19% in August as SVG activity surged. URL-delivered attacks more than doubled in September, reclaiming 30% of attacks.

PDF attachments declined from 22% of attacks in July to 12% in August, remaining at 12% in September.

HTML attachments declined from 9% of attacks in July to 2% in August, then more than tripled in volume in September to account for 6% of attacks.

DOC/DOCX attachments remained comparatively uncommon throughout Q3, representing only 1% of attacks each month.

Figure 7. CAPTCHA-gated phishing distribution method share by month (April – September 2026)

Malicious payloads

The dominant risk from malicious attachments continued to be credential theft, not malware installation. Approximately 94-96% of payload-based attacks during Q3 directed recipients toward a phishing site or presented a fraudulent sign-in page locally. An attachment did not need to install software to put an account at risk.

HTML and PDF attachments remained the two most common malicious payload types during Q3, together accounting for approximately 56–62% of payload-based attacks each month, while the more significant change was the return of SVG files:

Figure 8. Malicious payloads by type

HTML attachments accounted for nearly two-thirds of malicious payloads and remained relatively steady across the quarter. HTML files ranked first in July at 32% of attacks before declining to 26% in August and recovering to 29% in September.

PDF attachments accounted for 27–30% of attacks and were the leading payload type in August and September. Volume remained comparatively stable, declining only 2% between July and September.

SVG attachments increased from 13% of attacks in July to 20% in August, when volume reached 10.1 million—the highest monthly volume in more than a year. Volume then fell 34% in September, although SVGs still represented 13% of attacks and remained roughly 50% higher than the monthly average for the first half of 2026.

DOC/DOCX attachments declined from approximately 5% of attacks in July and August to less than 3% in September, falling 76% below its monthly average volume for the first half of 2026.

ZIP/GZIP attachments declined from 5% of attacks in July to 3% in August before recovering slightly to 4% in September. Raw volume remained 24% below July.

The reduced use of Word documents alongside the renewed use of SVG files left a different mix of attachment threats, though credential theft remained the dominant objective.

Figure 9. Malicious payload file type distribution by month (June – September 2026)

CAPTCHA-gated phishing accounted for only part of the malicious SVG activity. The resurgence was therefore broader than the use of SVG files to deliver that particular technique.

Business contact impersonation

Microsoft defines business contact impersonation (BCI) as a text-based attack targeting enterprise users that impersonates a trusted entity for the purpose of persuading a recipient into initiating a fraudulent financial transaction or sending the attacker sensitive documents.

BCI volume declined throughout Q3, totaling approximately 6.2 million attacks. That was substantially below Q2, although the comparison is influenced by the unusually large spike in April. By September, monthly activity had fallen to its lowest level since at least July 2025.

Figure 10. Monthly BCI attack volume (January – September 2026)

The reduction in overall volume also concealed differences among financial lures. Generic messages continued to dominate initial BCI contact during Q3, but explicit task and financial requests gained share as overall attack volume declined:

Generic outreach messages, such as “Are you at your desk?”, accounted for 82% of attacks in July and August before declining to 79% in September. Raw volume fell 14% across the quarter, reinforcing that operators still overwhelmingly favored establishing contact before introducing a fraudulent request.

Generic task requests represented 8–10% of attacks during Q3, increasing from 9% in July to 10% in September despite a 9% decline in raw volume.

Within the smaller subset of explicit financial requests:

Payroll update requests were the most common financial lure, accounting for 6% of attacks in July and August and 7% in September. Raw volume remained broadly stable at approximately 126,000–130,000 attacks per month.

Invoice payment requests recovered from June’s low. Volume increased 34% in July, 25% in August, and 89% in September, more than tripling between June and September. Their share reached 3% in September, its highest level since March.

Gift card requests remained at 2% of attacks each month, while raw volume declined 9% from July to September.

Figure 11. Initial BCI email content by type (Q3 2026)

The decline in BCI overall did not extend equally to the requests reaching payment and payroll staff.

Microsoft Teams threats

Microsoft observed approximately 141,000 malicious Teams call attempts during Q3. Activity peaked in July before declining 31% by September, although September volume remained 38% above the monthly average for the first half of 2026. Teams-based attacks continued to use live interactions across chat, voice, screen sharing, and remote-support tools to facilitate remote access, credential theft, and hands-on-keyboard compromise.

Figure 12. Monthly observed malicious Microsoft Teams calls (January – September 2026)

Attackers increasingly moved away from display names that explicitly announced an IT- or tech-related support role. Ordinary personal-name display names rose from 46% of the observed July sample to 88% in September, while explicit help desk identities fell from 17% to 2%.

Figure 13. Malicious Teams call impersonation comparison (Q3 2026)

This shift does not necessarily mean attackers abandoned IT support stories. A personal name can accompany a claim to work for the help desk, while the underlying account address retains technical or service-related wording. More targeted attempts also used domains resembling the intended victim organization’s domain, emphasizing that the visible name is only one part of the impersonation.

Voice phishing attempts peaked in July and then receded, but September volume remained above the levels observed early in 2026. Calls were concentrated during recipients’ weekday working hours, when a live response was more likely. These attempts included unanswered, rejected, and short-lived calls, partly reflecting Microsoft’s expanding visibility and ongoing efforts to strengthen protective measures against social engineering abuse. Attemps should not be interpreted as successful attacker interactions.

Notable phishing campaigns

The following campaigns were observed during the quarter and highlight notable credential phishing, BCI, and malware delivery activity. For analysis of a separate Teams-based IT-support impersonation campaign observed in August, see Impersonating IT support: Threat actors turn remote session into enterprise-wide access.

Salary review lure delivers personalized QR code attachment for device code credential capture targeting legal organizations

On August 19, 2026, Microsoft Defender Research observed a phishing campaign targeting more than 10,000 users across more than 4,800 organizations, almost exclusively located in the United States. While most phishing attacks typically don’t focus on a single vertical, this campaign targeted the professional services sector, specifically law firms and legal organizations. Messages in this campaign were sent out over a 13-hour period between 13:27 UTC on August 19, 2026, and 2:59 UTC on August 20, 2026.

Figure 14. Intended campaign targets by industry

Emails in this campaign were sent with the subject line “Salary Review” from smtp[@]wekash[.]net via Amazon Simple Email Service. The email body carried no visible text and the sole payload was a Word document attachment named Your-Q3-Compensation-Summary.docx.

Figure 15. Sample of the campaign document attachment

The Word document impersonated the recipient’s own organization, displaying company branding and addressing the recipient by name. The message claimed that the recipient’s compensation had been revised following a Q2 performance review and that updated details were ready for review. A QR code in the document carried an instruction to scan it to access the revised details. This approach moved the phishing URL out of the email body and into an image, bypassing email gateway controls that scan text-based links but do not decode QR code images.

Scanning the QR code would have directed users to an attacker-controlled phishing page impersonating a Microsoft OneDrive sign-in portal hosted on the domain splace[.]co[.]za. The page presented an alphanumeric code and instructed recipients to copy it and proceed to the Microsoft sign-in portal.

Figure 16. Sample phishing landing page

The phishing page used a device code phishing technique, which works by making an authentication request to Microsoft’s device authentication service before the recipient arrived, receiving a user code in return, and embedding that code into the page. When a recipient copied the code and proceeded, the page redirected them to the legitimate Microsoft device authentication portal at microsoft.com/devicelogin, where they entered the code and signed in. Completing that sign in would have transferred a valid session token to the attacker. The token granted persistent access to the recipient’s Microsoft 365 account without ever exposing the password and without re-triggering multifactor authentication (MFA). A countdown timer on the page signaled that each code had a limited validity window, pressing recipients to act quickly.

Spanish-language purchase order and payroll campaign leads to Agent Tesla malware

On September 21, 2026, Microsoft Defender Research observed a phishing campaign targeting more than 56,000 users across more than 8,100 organizations. The campaign primarily targeted users in Spanish-speaking countries, with Colombia accounting for the largest share of intended recipients (15%), followed by the United States (12%), Mexico (12%), Chile (11%), and Spain (8%). Like most large-scale phishing attacks, this campaign did not focus on a single vertical, but instead targeted a broad range of industries, most notably retail and consumer goods (27%), manufacturing and agriculture (19%), and financial services (13%). Messages in this campaign were sent out over an almost nine-hour period between 14:57 UTC and 23:35 UTC on September 21, 2026.

Figure 17. Timeline of campaign message volume

Two lure variations were observed throughout the duration of the campaign: a purchase order theme, which was used in 63% of messages, and a payroll theme, which was used in the remaining 37%. Both variations were sent from the address contacto06[@]carloxmextos[.]org. Sender Policy Framework (SPF), DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM), and Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) all passed for that domain, so the messages did not depend on simple address forgery. The actor changed the display name to resemble a sales or human resources identity associated with the recipient’s organization. That combination gave the messages technically valid authentication while using the visible sender identity and familiar business context to support the impersonation.

The purchase order lure variation used the reply-style subject “Re: solicitud de cotización”. Its body said, “Buen Dia”, claimed that a purchase order was attached, and asked the recipient to confirm receipt before closing with the lowercase “saludos”. The abrupt wording, inconsistent capitalization, and copied professional signature made the message look like a short continuation of an existing commercial exchange while avoiding details that a recipient could easily challenge.

The attached file, Nuevo orden de compra – 21092026.pdf.uu, was a RAR archive despite its uncommon .uu ending and PDF-like name. Inside it was Nuevo orden de compra – 21092026.pdf.js, a JavaScript downloader whose second extension exposed the executable script type only after extraction. If run, the script fetched a file named Lincoln.ps1 from a campaign-controlled object in Firebase Storage, and that PowerShell payload led to Agent Tesla malware. The nested archive and misleading extensions separated the visible business document theme from the code that executed, while the cloud-hosted download gave the actor a remotely accessible staging point.

Figure 18. Redacted rendering of the purchase order lure email

The payroll-themed lure used the subject “Nomina 21.09.2026”. It addressed the recipient by name, said the September 21 payroll list was attached, and signed off as a human resources manager. The date-specific payroll pretext created an immediate work-related reason to open the file, while the personalized greeting made a bulk message appear locally relevant.

The payroll lure’s attachment, Nomina 21.09.2026.xml.001, was also a RAR archive. Extraction produced Nomina 21.09.2026.xml.exe, an Agent Tesla executable disguised with an XML-themed double extension. Unlike the purchase order delivery chain, this branch did not require a separate downloader in the supplied evidence, but both paths used the same sender infrastructure, attachment camouflage, date, and malware family. Agent Tesla is commonly used to collect credentials and other information from an infected host, so the shared final payload suggested that credential and information theft were the campaign’s likely objective.

Figure 19. Redacted rendering of the payroll lure email

Defending against email and collaboration threats

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

Microsoft helps organizations reduce the risk of phishing and social engineering in Teams through user awareness and layered, built-in protections. Users should exercise caution with external connection requests and messages, including verifying a sender’s identity and requests before acting on them. Administrators can also block external Teams users and specify which users in their organization are permitted to chat or meet with people outside the enterprise. These flexible controls help organizations manage risk for employees in sensitive roles and departments. Teams will also be introducing AI-powered phishing detection that uses conversation context to identify phishing and social engineering in higher-risk messaging scenarios, particularly first-contact chats with external users. Together, these measures help organizations collaborate more securely in Teams.

Review the recommended settings for Exchange Online Protection and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to ensure your organization has established essential defenses and knows how to monitor and respond to threat activity.

Invest in user awareness training and phishing simulations. Attack simulation training in Microsoft Defender for Office 365, which also includes simulating phishing messages in Microsoft Teams, is one approach to running realistic attack scenarios in your organization.

Enable Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) in Defender for Office 365 to quarantine sent mail in response to newly acquired threat intelligence and retroactively neutralize malicious phishing, spam, or malware messages that have already been delivered to mailboxes.

Responders can also manually check for and purge unwanted emails containing URLs and/or Subject fields that are similar, but not identical, to those of known bad messages. Investigate malicious email that was delivered in Microsoft 365 and use Threat Explorer to find and delete phishing emails.

Turn on Safe Links and Safe Attachments in Microsoft Defender for Office 365.

Enable network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.

Encourage users to use Microsoft Edge and other web browsers that support Microsoft Defender SmartScreen, which identifies and blocks malicious websites, including phishing sites, scam sites, and sites that host malware.

Enable passwordless authentication methods (for example, Windows Hello, FIDO keys, or Microsoft Authenticator) for accounts that support passwordless. For accounts that still require passwords, use authenticator apps like Microsoft Authenticator for MFA. Refer to this article for the different authentication methods and features.

Conditional access policies can also be scoped to strengthen privileged accounts with phishing-resistant MFA.

Configure automatic attack disruption in Microsoft Defender XDR. Automatic attack disruption is designed to contain attacks in progress, limit the impact on an organization’s assets, and provide more time for security teams to remediate the attack fully.

Microsoft Defender coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, and apps to provide integrated protection against attacks like the threat discussed in this blog.

In this article

Attack chain overview

Mitigation and protection guidance

Learn More

Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified an evolving fake-download campaign targeting users searching for cracked commercial software, free games, activators, plugins, and unofficial utilities. The campaign uses trojanized Inno Setup-style installers to distribute multiple monetized software payloads, referred to by the delivery system as “offers”, during a single installation session.

Our investigation found that the installers use a per-offer callback and status-tracking model to manage delivery and record installation outcomes. We confirmed three downstream monetization branches that transformed affected devices into monetized assets, including by routing third-party internet traffic through the device, enrolling it in a distributed-computing platform, or installing additional utility-style software, often without users’ informed knowledge or consent. These products and components may have legitimate uses, but their silent installation through deceptive software bundles without informed user consent introduces security and privacy risks.

Organizations can reduce their exposure to this activity by preventing the use of untrusted software sources, enabling potentially unwanted application protection, and monitoring for unexpected software installations and persistence mechanisms.

This blog details the campaign’s execution model and confirmed outcomes and provides mitigation guidance, Microsoft Defender protection information, advanced hunting queries, MITRE ATT&CK mappings, and indicators of compromise to help defenders identify, investigate, and respond to related activity.

Attack chain overview

The fake-download campaign follows a four-stage attack chain that progresses from deceptive lures through Inno-based staging, offer-controlled payload delivery, and installation of one or more monetization branches:

Initial access via fake download lures – Users run fake installers promoted as cracked commercial software, free games, activators, plugins, executors, or unofficial utilities.

Inno wrapper execution and temporary runner staging – The installer launches an Inno Setup-style temporary runner under %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\, which starts recurring eld*.exe, set_*.exe, or other numbered stages.

Offer execution callback and payload delivery – The runner contacts rotating infrastructure using a repeatable d=inno and r=offer_execution callback pattern. Offer, affiliate, download-network, placement, and session values coordinate downstream payload selection and correlate activity within the installer session.

Final payload installation and monetization – Staged payloads use unattended installation switches to install one or more confirmed campaign branches: WorldProxyPool for proxy and network-resource monetization; CharityEngine and Berkeley Open Infrastructure for Network Computing (BOINC) for compute-resource monetization; or Advanced Windows (AW) Manager and Windows Manager for adware-style utility monetization. WorldProxyPool also creates recurring SYSTEM scheduled tasks for agent startup, watchdog execution, and updater activity.

Attack Chain

Figure 1. Overview of the attack chain.

Initial access via fake download lures

The campaign begins when users download and run fake installers promoted as cracked software, game installers, executors, activators, plugins, utilities, or driver and mobile-unlock tools. Observed lures include cracked audio plugins, PC games, Roblox executors, auto-clickers, driver tools, and fake utility installers.

Example lures: Echo Client; FabFilter Total Bundle; Navicat Premium crack; Cue Club; auto-clicker; Deadpool Apunka Games; Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2; TFT Unlock Tool; and clownfishvoicechanger.

Figure 2. Example utility download lure.

Inno wrapper execution and temporary runner staging

Across the investigated activity, user-launched lures spawned Inno Setup-style temporary runners under %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\ and then launched one or more numbered eld*.exe stages. Arguments such as /SL5, /SPAWNWND, and /FIRSTWND, together with the temporary path and numbered stage names, provide more durable indicators than the original lure filename.

The depth of the execution chain and its downstream outcome varied by installer session. One Echo Client example progressed through multiple numbered stages and reached several monetization branches, while other observed lures exposed fewer numbered stages or downstream components.

The table below uses the Echo Client activity as a representative example of the wrapper-to-stage sequence; individual installer sessions may launch different combinations of numbered stages.

Offer execution callback and payload delivery

After staging, the Inno temporary runner contacted rotating callback infrastructure using randomized URL paths but a repeatable query-string structure:

Failed or blocked offers used r=offer_execution_fail and sometimes included local error text, including messages that the operation did not complete because the file contained a virus or potentially unwanted software. These callbacks are useful campaign-attribution and sequencing markers, but they are not always the earliest prevention point. In some endpoint detection and response (EDR) traces, child payloads launched before or around the r=offer_execution callback.

The campaign used offer IDs, affiliate IDs, download-network IDs, and placement values to select or report downstream payload attempts. Different offers could succeed or fail independently within the same installer session, so a failed first offer did not necessarily mean that the full bundle stopped.

Final payload installation and monetization

After offer callback and payload delivery, the campaign launched downstream installers or components using unattended installation switches such as /qn, /S, /quiet, and /norestart. This stage converted the fake-download execution chain into installed software and recurring execution across three monetization branches: proxy and network-resource monetization, compute-resource monetization, and adware-style utility monetization.

Proxy and network-resource monetization — WorldProxyPool

In the WorldProxyPool branch, a staged eld4.exe payload created three SYSTEM-level scheduled tasks for components under C:\Program Files\WorldProxyPool\. WorldProxyPoolAgent configured sdk-agent.exe to run at system startup with highest privileges; WorldProxyPoolWatchdog configured a hidden, noninteractive PowerShell watchdog script to run every five minutes; and WorldProxyPoolUpdater configured sdk-agent.updater.exe update to run hourly. The installer also started the agent task immediately with schtasks.exe /Run. Subsequent task launches were brokered by the Windows Task Scheduler service (svchost.exe -k netsvcs -p -s Schedule), causing sdk-agent.exe and the watchdog script to execute in the service context. This persistence mechanism supports recurring proxy-agent, watchdog, and updater activity, consistent with network-resource monetization.

Compute-resource monetization — CharityEngine and BOINC

In the CharityEngine and BOINC branch, the offer payload installed distributed-compute software and supporting components under C:\Program Files\BOINC\ and C:\ProgramData\BOINC\. Observed components included ce-installer_7.14.2_vbox-7.2.8.exe, ce_7.14.2_windows_x86_64.exe, charityengine.exe, boinc.exe, boinctray.exe, boinc.scr, boincscr.exe, wrapper_2022110901_windows_x86_64.exe, ce11.exe, and VirtualBox-7.2.8-r173730.msi. Adware-style utility monetization: AdvancedWindowsManager / Windows Manager

The same Inno offer-execution infrastructure delivered an AW Manager or Windows Manager branch. In one observed process tree, the Inno runner spawned eld3.exe, launched Windows Manager – Postback Johan.msi, and installed AdvancedWindowsManager.exe and Windows Updater.exe under paths resembling %APPDATA%\AW Manager\Windows Manager 1.0.0\ or C:\Program Files (x86)\AW Manager\Windows Manager\.

Figure 5. AW Manager / Windows Manager utility-install branch.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft recommends the following actions to reduce exposure to this campaign and detect related activity:

Preventive controls

Avoid untrusted software sources. Do not download cracked software, key generators, unofficial game installers, or software activation tools, which are common delivery mechanisms for malware, potentially unwanted applications, and monetization campaigns.

Enable cloud-delivered protection. Verify that Microsoft Defender Antivirus cloud-delivered protection is enabled to improve detection of emerging malware and potentially unwanted applications. See: Configure cloud-delivered protection

Keep tamper protection enabled. Use tamper protection to help prevent unauthorized changes to Microsoft Defender security settings. See: Learn about tamper protection.

Enable reputation-based protection. Configure reputation-based protection to help block known malicious and untrusted applications and downloads. See: Configure reputation-based protection.

Consider Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) protections. Evaluate ASR rules, including rules that block executable files unless they meet prevalence, age, or trusted-list criteria. See: Review Attack Surface Reduction rules.

Investigation actions

Investigate execution from Inno temporary directories. Review activity from paths such as %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\, particularly when staged executables such as eld*.exe, set_*.exe, FirstFast[1].exe, or SecondRunner[1].exe are observed.

Correlate Inno callback activity. Monitor outbound requests containing d=inno together with r=offer_execution or r=offer_execution_fail, and review related process, file, and network activity across the complete installer session.

Review unexpected scheduled tasks. Investigate newly created scheduled tasks, particularly tasks running with SYSTEM privileges or recurring watchdog and updater functions. See: Audit scheduled task creation events.

Audit software inventory for unexpected installations. Review endpoints for the presence of software such as WorldProxyPool, CharityEngine, BOINC, VirtualBox, or other applications that users did not intentionally install. See: Review software inventory in Defender Vulnerability Management.

Microsoft Defender XDR detections

Microsoft Defender detects and blocks campaign-linked payloads through cloud protection, machine-learning classifications, network inspection, and behavior monitoring. Relevant observed detections include remote-thread injection, scheduled-task launch, and suspicious outbound HTTP activity.

Customers with provisioned access can also use Microsoft Security Copilot in Microsoft Defender to investigate and respond to incidents, hunt for threats, and protect their organization with relevant threat intelligence.

The reporting helps analysts correlate offer callbacks and endpoint activity from the same installer session, identify devices with associated monetization stages, and assess the overall bundle outcome. It also provides investigation context, protection guidance, relevant indicators, and recommended response actions.

articles.title: What exploited vulnerabilities have in common: A data-driven analysis of real-world attacks
articles.context: Microsoft Security helps defenders discover the doors threat actors can see, prioritize the weaknesses they are most likely to exploit, understand where a compromise could lead,...
articles.full_text:
In this article

Classifying the vulnerability landscape

Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild

Where defenders should focus

Patching is slow, while exploitation is fast

Impact, exposure and where to focus

Next in line

How Microsoft Security helps defenders act

References

Learn More

The vulnerability landscape continues to expand. From 1999 through September 2026, approximately 383,000 software vulnerabilities had been disclosed across platforms and technologies, yet only about 2,000 CVEs (roughly 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation.

Those vulnerabilities follow clear patterns. Threat actors disproportionately target flaws that enable system takeover, particularly remote code execution, privilege escalation, and authentication bypass. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploit development could further shorten the window defenders have to respond.

Patching remains essential, but remediation can take weeks or months on critical systems, and some legacy or unsupported systems cannot be patched. Defenders therefore need to concentrate protection where it can have the greatest impact, considering both the likelihood of exploitation and the potential blast radius of a successful attack.

Classifying the vulnerability landscape

To make this large vulnerability population actionable, we analyzed each CVE across two dimensions: impact class and affected platform.

Impact class captures the outcome a threat actor could achieve by exploiting a vulnerability. Each CVE is assigned to the most consequential impact it directly enables. For example, when a vulnerability can bypass authentication and directly enable remote code execution (RCE), we classify it as RCE. This approach helps distinguish the underlying type of vulnerability from the security impact an attacker could achieve.

Server-side RCE: Remote code execution on a network-exposed service without user interaction.

Client-side RCE: Remote code execution that requires a user to open or run malicious content.

Local code execution: Code or command execution requiring local access or an existing foothold.

Local privilege escalation: Elevation from lower-level access to SYSTEM or root privileges.

Authentication or authorization bypass: Circumvention of authentication or access controls.

Security-control bypass: Circumvention of protections such as sandboxing, secure boot, or SmartScreen.

Information disclosure: Exposure of sensitive data or secrets.

Tampering or integrity: Unauthorized modification of data or system state.

Denial of service: Disruption of system or service availability.

Cross-site scripting (XSS): Script execution within a victim’s browser context.

Arbitrary file access: Unauthorized access to or placement of files.

Spoofing or redirect: Spoofing, redirection, or other forms of UI deception.

We also classified vulnerabilities by the platforms they affect, including Windows, Linux/Unix, mobile, network appliances, IoT/OT, virtualization hosts, and developer packages. A CVE can span multiple platforms. Developer packages are treated as a separate category because they are often cross-platform and represent a significant share of the overall vulnerability population.

Most CVEs in the analysis affect application code, including servers, web applications, browsers, productivity software, libraries, and firmware tooling, while a smaller share affects OS and system code such as kernels, drivers, and firmware.

This analysis covers CVEs published through September 2026 using Microsoft’s catalog of tracked vulnerabilities. Each CVE is counted once in the impact analysis and across each relevant platform in the platform analysis.

Figure 1 – The full published-CVE population as of September 2026, broken down by impact class and affected platform, and an OS vs. application split. Breadth dominates – many impact classes spread across many platforms, with about 77% of CVEs in application code and 23% in OS/system code.

Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild

The subset of vulnerabilities exploited in the wild is much smaller than the overall CVE population, and looks very different from it. Fewer than 1 in 200 published CVEs are ever used in a real attack, and those that do get used are overwhelmingly concentrated in the takeover classes that maximize threat actor impact and exposure.

The difference becomes clear when we look at impact. Exploitation is heavily concentrated in vulnerabilities that give attackers greater control over a system. Server-side RCE rises from 20% of published CVEs to 37% of exploited CVEs, local privilege escalation from 11% to 18%, and client-side RCE from 4% to 13%. By comparison, XSS falls from 15% to 4% and denial of service from 16% to 7%. OS vulnerabilities show a similar shift, increasing from 23% of the overall CVE population to 41% of exploited vulnerabilities.

These patterns are consistent with threat actors favoring vulnerabilities that can provide meaningful access and control. Remote code execution and privilege escalation can create footholds that support subsequent stages of an attack, while vulnerabilities that primarily cause a crash or limited script execution may offer less utility for broader compromise.

Importantly, a vulnerability’s stated classification does not always reflect what an attacker can reliably achieve in practice. For example, some vulnerabilities described as enabling RCE may ultimately result only in denial of service under real-world conditions. Understanding the demonstrated impact and exploitability of a vulnerability is therefore critical to effective prioritization.

Figure 2 – The 2,056 exploited-in-the-wild CVEs distribution, compared against the full published population: ghost lines mark each class and platform’s share of all ~380K published CVEs, and badges show the shift in percentage points. Takeover classes and OS code rise, while high-volume XSS and DoS fall.

Where defenders should focus

Patching is slow, while exploitation is fast

Patching is slow, and far slower on critical systems than others. Across platforms, servers are the critical assets and the slowest to patch. Microsoft Security Exposure Management data from 2026 shows that the median vulnerability is patched in about two weeks on Windows workstations but in more than a month on Windows Servers. It stretches to 10+ weeks on Linux Servers and for applications running on MacOS, and beyond a year on network appliances. That gap is the threat actor’s window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest.

Exploitation runs on the opposite clock: the most impactful vulnerabilities are weaponized in days, increasingly on or before disclosure. According to VulnCheck, 29% of the exploits in 2025 were launched within 1 day of CVE publication. According to CISA, the mean time from CVE publication to CISA KEV catalog fell from 89 days in 2024 to 57 days in 2025. 2026 data up to September already have that number dropping to 20 days, with a median of only 3 days since publication. Industry research suggests that advances in AI are a significant factor in the time reduction required to develop exploits, further increasing pressure on defenders to respond quickly.

Impact, exposure and where to focus

Two things determine a vulnerability’s value to a threat actor: impact and exposure. Impact is what successful exploitation provides, such as remote code execution or privilege escalation. Exposure is an asset’s position in the environment and the opportunities it creates for further compromise. An asset’s exposure is shaped by the identities, privileges, and connections available from it.

Servers often use service accounts, application identities, or cloud-managed identities with permissions beyond their operational needs. Compromising such a system can provide access to additional resources, sensitive data, administrative privileges, or trusted network paths. Together, impact and exposure determine the blast radius: a vulnerability that enables full control of a highly exposed system can enable widespread on-premises or cloud compromise.

Threat actors do not exploit at random: they go after the vulnerabilities that give the highest impact and exposure: full control of a system and the privileged identities and critical assets it has access to. As defenders, focusing on these vulnerabilities first can deliver the highest return on remediation investment.

Takeover vulnerabilities like remote code execution, authentication bypass and local privilege escalation lead here. They drive the broadest exposure and the largest blast radius, account for 78% of real-world exploited vulnerabilities, and stopping their exploitation interrupts attacks at the earliest stage, before compromise can propagate across the environment.

Next in line

A second slice deserves attention where context makes it severe: denial of service against availability-critical assets is recoverable in general, but can be mission-ending in parts of your environment where uptime is everything; disclosure of credentials or secrets can be minor as an insulated incident, but it feeds the same privileged-identity path mentioned above.

Figure 3 – The three remote-takeover classes analyzed across 1,239 exploited CVEs), each drilled down by affected platform and split into OS vs Application code. Bar length is the CVE count per platform; the dark segment is OS/system, the light segment is application.

How Microsoft Security helps defenders act

Threat actors do not begin with a vulnerability list. They begin by looking for a reachable way in. Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management approaches the environment from that same outside-in perspective, continuously discovering internet-facing infrastructure, including previously unknown or unmonitored assets, shadow IT, and third-party dependencies. This gives defenders an opportunity to remove unnecessary exposure before a reachable vulnerability becomes an entry point.

Once the reachable assets are known, the next question is which weaknesses deserve immediate attention. Defenders need a way to prioritize exposure beyond CVSS alone. Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management addresses this challenge through Exposure Score and prioritized security recommendations.

Prioritization incorporates threat and exploitability signals, breach likelihood, internet exposure, and asset criticality, helping teams focus remediation on vulnerabilities that create the greatest actual exposure.

An initial foothold is only part of the risk. Attack Path Analysis connects assets and threat actor techniques into end-to-end routes from an entry point to a critical asset. Microsoft Security Exposure Management Attack Path Analysis provides a cross-workload view spanning endpoints, cloud, and hybrid environments, using vulnerability context from MDVM, endpoint data from Defender for Endpoint, and cloud asset data from Defender for Cloud. Within cloud environments, Defender CSPM Attack Path Analysis adds detailed context about internet exposure, vulnerabilities, network connections, identities, and permissions across Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud.

Together, these experiences show how an exposed workload could become a path through a privileged identity to sensitive data or another critical resource, helping defenders identify where to break the path before the initial compromise expands.

Patching remains essential, but it is not the only defensive action available. Microsoft Security helps defenders discover the doors threat actors can see, prioritize the weaknesses they are most likely to exploit, understand where a compromise could lead, and identify opportunities to break attack paths before compromise spreads to critical assets.

On October 29, 2026, Cursor reported that a tampered copy of Claude Code extension (anthropic.claude-code, versions 2.1.313 and 2.1.312) was available and served in the Cursor extension marketplace for a few hours to attempt a supply-chain attack on Cursor users. Cursor reports that it was live from about 2:27 AM to 1:35 PM Pacific Daylight Time (PDT). We have confirmed that the malicious packages found on Cursor marketplace were never published nor distributed from Microsoft Visual Studio Marketplace and from npm @antropic-ai/claude-code, which were not affected by this incident. Anthropic confirmed to Microsoft that their systems were not compromised and they did not develop the malicious package posted in Cursor marketplace. At this time, all evidence suggests that the incident is limited to Cursor marketplace.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence analyzed the injected JavaScript embedded in the malicious extension package. The injected loader runs when the extension module loads and attempts to add an attacker-controlled Secure Shell (SSH) key, enable the local SSH service, establish reverse SSH forwarding, configure persistence, and report host details. Successful remote access depends on host privileges, SSH configuration, and the attacker’s server configuration; however, the loader may still write keys and persistence artifacts even when tunnel access fails.

Organizations should identify systems that installed or automatically updated to this version from the Cursor marketplace, preserve evidence, remove confirmed malicious artifacts, review endpoint and network telemetry, and rotate credentials or revoke sessions when investigation indicates exposure. Microsoft customers can use the detections and hunting guidance in this post after the listed coverage and query validation gates are complete.

Attack chain overview

A malicious artifact associated with the Cursor Marketplace incident included a JavaScript function that executed before the extension’s expected code. When the module loads, this function can use Node.js APIs to collect host information, modify files, and execute operating-system commands. The following sections describe capabilities and attempted actions based on our analysis of the injected code.

Attack chain

The loader first collects host reconnaissance. It then attempts to install an SSH key, enable SSH, create a reverse tunnel, and configure persistence. A delayed callback subsequently attempts to send host details. The following sequence reflects code execution order; it does not prove that every step succeeded on every host.

Module loading and reconnaissance collection. The injected function executes before normal extension initialization and collects host and user information.

SSH access preparation. The loader appends an embedded public key and attempts to enable the local SSH service.

Reverse forwarding. An embedded tunnel identity authenticates an outbound connection that requests forwarding to the workstation’s SSH port.

Platform-specific persistence. Scripts and startup configuration are written to relaunch the connection.

Host reconnaissance reporting. After the access and persistence setup attempts, a delayed callback attempts to transmit the previously collected host details and selected environment-variable names.

Figure 1. Attack chain reconstructed from the injected code.

The loader uses embedded components and built-in system tools to establish persistent access without downloading another executable. It suppresses command output and silently catches errors to conceal failures and malicious activity, while the extension continues functioning normally to avoid alerting users.

Host reconnaissance collection

The loader collects the hostname, username, operating system, architecture, home directory, working directory, and global Git email. It also looks for environment-variable names containing terms such as KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASS, AWS, or GCP, keeping up to forty matches.

The callback sends matching environment-variable names, not values. This reveals potentially sensitive configuration categories but does not demonstrate theft of the secrets stored in those variables.

Collection occurs during module loading. The collected details are retained for the delayed reporting callback described after the persistence stage.

SSH authorization and tunnel identities

The loader uses two SSH identities with distinct roles. One public key authorizes access to the workstation’s user account, while a separate private key authenticates the outbound connection to the tunnel server. First, the loader checks the user’s authorized_keys file for the comment svc-telemetry. If the marker is missing, it appends an embedded Ed25519 public key. That creates an authorization entry for whoever holds the corresponding private key, subject to the local SSH server’s configuration.

Next, it decodes a separate private key for the outbound connection. The initial copy is written to a hidden temporary file named .stk_ followed by ten hexadecimal characters derived from the hostname and home directory. SSH receives that file through its -i option and connects using the remote account tunnel.

The public-key material is redacted but the format is similar to the following:

ssh-ed25519 [REDACTED PUBLIC KEY] svc-telemetry

Protocol Tunneling (T1572): reverse SSH forwarding

The tunneling SSH process is launched with the command line containing the following arguments:

-N -R '*:0:localhost:22'

It requests a listening port on the remote SSH server and forwards connections through the tunnel to port 22 on the victim’s loopback interface. The remote port value 0 asks the server to allocate a port; it does not change the local target from port 22. The -N option tells SSH not to run a command on the tunnel server.

This design starts with an outbound connection from the workstation rather than waiting for a direct inbound connection to it. The loader disables ordinary host-key checking, bypasses the normal known-hosts file, sets keepalives, and avoids interactive prompts. On Unix-like systems it prefers autossh, falling back to ssh; on Windows it uses a hidden PowerShell loop. The loops wait sixty seconds after SSH exits before retrying.

Figure 2. Terminal-style SSH command configuring an outbound reverse tunnel from a server-assigned remote port to the workstation’s local SSH service on port 22. Host-key verification is disabled, and the identity-file path is redacted.

A running SSH process does not necessarily mean the attacker gained access. Both the attacker’s server and the victim’s workstation must allow the connection, and server settings determine whether the tunnel is publicly reachable. Cursor reports that errors and administrator-permission requirements blocked SSH access on most macOS and Windows hosts. However, the malware could still attempt to plant its SSH key, establish persistence, and report host information.

Platform-specific startup persistence

The loader writes platform-specific scripts and startup configuration outside the extension directory. The following table summarizes these mechanisms and their associated artifacts. The code attempts to configure persistence, but the presence of an artifact alone does not establish that the startup mechanism ran successfully.

Platform

Startup mechanism

Key artifacts

macOS

User LaunchAgent with RunAtLoad and KeepAlive

~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist, ~/.config/.smt,~/.config/.smtk

Linux

User-crontab @reboot entry

~/.config/.smt, ~/.config/.smtk

Windows

Attempted SysMon scheduled task requesting SYSTEM execution

%USERPROFILE%\.config\smt.cmd, %USERPROFILE%\.config\smtk

Windows fallback

Batch file in the user’s Startup folder

%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\sysmon.cmd

On Unix-like systems, the .smt script reconstructs the persistent .smtk identity when it runs, then starts its own SSH retry loop. On Windows, the loader writes the identity and batch script directly.

The startup objects use names such as SysMon and com.apple.sysmond, which resemble monitoring components. Behind these names, their configured actions invoke the generated scripts that maintain reverse SSH forwarding.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Immediate actions

Run advanced hunting queries below to identify affected systems and investigate systems where users installed or automatically updated anthropic.claude-code version 2.1.313 and 2.1.312 through the Cursor Extension Marketplace. Review extension-installation records and correlate endpoint, network, file, process, and authentication telemetry with the published indicators. Preserve the extension package, modified SSH authorization files, generated keys and scripts, and startup configuration before cleanup. Isolate devices with evidence of loader execution or backdoor installation.

Remediation actions

After evidence collection, check the affected user’s ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on macOS and Linux for the attacker-controlled key labeled svc-telemetry. On Windows, check both %USERPROFILE%\.ssh\authorized_keys and C:\ProgramData\ssh\administrators_authorized_keys, where present. Confirm the key against the fingerprint in Indicators of Compromise before removing the exact unauthorized entry. Preserve unrelated SSH keys and legitimate remote-development configuration. A missing marker alone should not replace review of the installation, process, network, and persistence evidence.

Remove the trojanized extension and confirmed malicious persistence after evidence collection. Inspect each startup object’s configured action before removal; names alone are not sufficient to distinguish malicious objects from legitimate monitoring software.

macOS: Unload and remove the malicious user LaunchAgent at ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist and remove its associated ~/.config/.smt script and ~/.config/.smtk identity.

Linux: Remove the malicious user-crontab @reboot entry referencing ~/.config/.smt, preserving unrelated entries, and remove the associated script and ~/.config/.smtk identity.

Windows: Remove the malicious SysMon scheduled task, the Startup-folder sysmon.cmd fallback, and associated %USERPROFILE%\.config\smt.cmd and %USERPROFILE%\.config\smtk files.

All applicable platforms: Stop confirmed malicious SSH and retry processes and remove their temporary .stk_ identity files after collection.

Cursor published platform-specific checks and remediation scripts in its security notice. Review the scripts and execution requirements before use, then verify that no listed artifacts remain. Cleanup does not replace investigation of device activity during the exposure window.

Removing or updating the extension does not remove artifacts written outside its installation directory. Remove confirmed unauthorized SSH keys, tunnel identities, scripts, and startup entries separately. Cursor’s reported server takedown does not remove artifacts already present on a device.

Follow-up Investigation and recovery

Review telemetry after the extension loaded for SSH key acceptance, tunnel processes, local SSH sessions, command execution, and file activity. Rotate credentials and revoke sessions from a known-clean device when telemetry indicates credential access or when device trust cannot be restored. Rebuild the device when required by the investigation and verify that the tunnel and startup artifacts do not return after login or restart.

To reduce the risk of malicious extensions and extension-based supply chain attacks, organizations using Cursor should apply the relevant controls in Cursor’s security-hardening guidance, including restricting extensions to approved publishers and configuring an extension installation cooldown to delay installation of newly published versions. These measures can help limit exposure to malicious releases.

Advanced hunting queries

The following queries use the Microsoft Defender XDR advanced hunting schema and the time range selected in the portal. A result is an investigative lead, not proof of compromise.

Connections to the reported infrastructure

Find network events involving the reported IP address during the last 30 days, including the process responsible for each connection.

DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RemoteIP == "134.209.82.225" or RemoteUrl has "134.209.82.225" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl

Reported malicious file and persistence artifacts

Find file events matching the reported SHA-256 hash, artifact filenames, or filename prefix during the last 30 days. Filename matches are hunting leads and require investigation.

DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 == "ecb58cb29078d9646ad1dcdbe51526f2d9cfea06be5fb2ab183e8ecc3ab6bf15" or FileName in~ ( ".smt", ".smtk", "smt.cmd", "smtk", "sysmon.cmd", "com.apple.sysmond.plist" ) or FileName startswith ".stk_" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

SHA-256 values might not be populated for every file event. The filename and prefix conditions provide additional hunting leads.

Possible Windows scheduled-task persistence

Find scheduled-task creation events whose additional fields contain both reported terms, SysMon and smt, during the last 30 days.

DeviceEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where ActionType == "ScheduledTaskCreated" | where AdditionalFields has "SysMon" and AdditionalFields has "smt" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AdditionalFields, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

Possible macOS LaunchAgent persistence

Find plist-property modification events whose FolderPath matches the reported com.apple.sysmond.plist artifact.

DeviceEvents | where ActionType == "PlistPropertyModified" | where FolderPath has "com.apple.sysmond.plist"
